issues.legal_issue: A statutory summary proceeding for recovery of company property is a form of due process and may be used consistently with an injunction barring dispossession except by due process.
material_facts: A civil court had ordered that the occupants not be dispossessed except by due process of law.
The company pursued a statutory criminal proceeding that could result in an order for delivery of its property.
issues.conclusion: The statutory proceeding was a procedure established by law and was not excluded by the injunction; the company was not required to rely only on a civil suit to obtain possession.
issues.legal_principle: The relevant provision supplies a summary legal remedy to recover company property, including an order for delivery of possession. Due process means a procedure established by law. The Court relied on Atul Mathur v. Atul Kalra and Abhilash Vinodkumar Jain v. Cox & Kings (India) Ltd. concerning the remedial purpose of the provision, and Lalita Jalan v. Bombay Gas Co. Ltd. concerning its quasi-criminal character and purpose.

predicates.company_property_recovery_proceeding: A company pursued a proceeding to recover its property from an occupant.
predicates.injunction_allows_dispossession_by_due_p: A court order barred dispossession except through due process of law.
predicates.proceeding_is_established_by_law: The recovery proceeding followed a procedure established by law.

issues.definition: When a company pursues a legally established property-recovery proceeding under an injunction permitting dispossession by due process, the proceeding satisfies that requirement.

issues.legal_issue: A company's civil action for possession does not prevent it from pursuing a separate statutory prosecution concerning wrongful retention of the same property.
material_facts: The company brought a civil suit seeking possession of the flat.
The company also filed a complaint alleging wrongful withholding of the flat.
issues.conclusion: The civil suit did not deprive the company of its right to institute the prosecution and seek a possession order through that proceeding.
issues.legal_principle: The statutory remedy provides a summary route for recovering company property, and filing a civil suit does not exclude that remedy. The Court relied on the remedial interpretation of the provision in Atul Mathur v. Atul Kalra and Abhilash Vinodkumar Jain v. Cox & Kings (India) Ltd.

predicates.company_property_recovery_prosecution: A company pursued a prosecution alleging wrongful retention of its property.
predicates.parallel_civil_possession_suit: The company also brought a civil suit seeking possession of the same property.

issues.definition: When a company pursues both a property-recovery prosecution and a civil possession suit, the civil action does not eliminate the statutory recovery remedy.

issues.legal_issue: Family members who continue to occupy company property after an employee's death wrongfully withhold it when their claimed permission rests on an unauthorized assurance by the company's chairman and they do not leave after notice.
material_facts: The flat belonged to the company and had been provided to an employee for residential use during his employment.
After the employee died, his family members remained in the flat although they were not company employees.
The company's chairman had assured the family members that they could remain until another flat was made available, but the Board had not authorized him to give that assurance.
The company demanded that the occupants vacate, but they continued to occupy the flat.
The lower courts found that the chairman had given the assurance, but the Supreme Court found no evidence that the Board had authorized it.
issues.conclusion: The chairman's assurance did not bind the company; the occupants wrongfully withheld the flat after the demand to vacate and committed the offence, for which each was fined.
issues.legal_principle: The relevant provision's clause concerning wrongful withholding applies where property lawfully provided during employment is retained after employment ends; the provision extends to former employees and their legal representatives. Under Section 291 of the Companies Act, directors act collectively as the Board, and an individual chairman has no authority to bind the company unless authority has been delegated, subject to the company's governing documents and law. The Court relied on Baldev Krishna Sahi v. Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. and Amrit Lal Chum v. Devoprasad Dutta Roy on the inclusion of former employees; Abhilash Vinodkumar Jain v. Cox & Kings (India) Ltd. on legal heirs and the provision's remedial character; Atul Mathur v. Atul Kalra on purposive interpretation; and Lalita Jalan v. Bombay Gas Co. Ltd. on the provision's quasi-criminal character.

rule.if: company_property_recovery_prosecution and company_owned_housing and family_member_retained_company_housing and employment_ended and chairman_assurance_given and no_board_authorization and vacate_notice_ignored

predicates.company_property_recovery_prosecution: A company pursued a prosecution alleging wrongful retention of its property.
predicates.company_owned_housing: The company owned residential property that it had made available to an employee for use during employment.
predicates.family_member_retained_company_housing: A family member of the employee remained in the company's housing after the employee's death.
predicates.employment_ended: The employee's service with the company ended before the family member's continued occupation.
predicates.chairman_assurance_given: The company's chairman told the family member that the family member could continue to occupy the property.
predicates.no_board_authorization: The Board had not authorized the chairman to make that assurance on the company's behalf.
predicates.vacate_notice_ignored: The company demanded that the occupant leave and the occupant continued to stay.

issues.definition: When family members retain company housing after the employee's service ends, and continue to occupy it after notice in reliance on an assurance the chairman lacked authority to give, they wrongfully withhold the property.

issues.legal_issue: A later court arrangement recognizing an occupant's possession does not extinguish liability for wrongful retention that occurred before that arrangement.
material_facts: The complaint alleged wrongful withholding before the civil court appointed a receiver.
The receiver was later given symbolic possession, while the occupant remained in actual possession as the receiver's agent.
issues.conclusion: The later receiver order did not wipe out the offence already committed; the occupants had wrongfully withheld the property before that order.
issues.legal_principle: The relevant provision addresses wrongful withholding and permits a court to order delivery of company property. A later change in the legal arrangement governing possession does not erase wrongful withholding that had already occurred. The Court applied the provision's distinction between the prior withholding and the later receiver arrangement.

predicates.company_property_recovery_prosecution: A company pursued a prosecution alleging wrongful retention of its property.
predicates.wrongful_retention_preceded_receiver_ord: The occupant wrongfully retained the property before a court made a later order concerning possession.
predicates.receiver_order_followed_complaint: After the complaint, a court placed the property in a receiver's symbolic possession and allowed the occupant to remain as the receiver's agent.

issues.definition: When wrongful retention preceded a later court arrangement placing property with a receiver, the earlier retention remains actionable.

issues.legal_issue: A criminal court cannot order delivery of actual possession while a civil court's receiver arrangement gives the occupant actual possession as the receiver's agent.
material_facts: A civil court appointed a receiver and placed the flat in the receiver's symbolic possession.
The civil court appointed the occupant as the receiver's agent to remain in actual possession during the suit.
issues.conclusion: While that order remained in force, no direction could be made in the prosecution for delivery of actual possession to the company; the company could seek suitable relief from the civil court.
issues.legal_principle: The relevant provision allows the court trying the offence to order delivery of company property, but the Court held that such an order for actual possession could not be made while the civil court's receiver arrangement remained in force. The company remained free to apply to the civil court for suitable orders.

predicates.company_property_recovery_prosecution: A company pursued a prosecution alleging wrongful retention of its property.
predicates.receiver_has_symbolic_possession: A civil court placed the property in a receiver's symbolic possession.
predicates.occupant_is_receiver_agent: The civil court allowed the occupant to remain in actual possession as the receiver's agent.

issues.definition: When a receiver holds symbolic possession and the occupant remains as the receiver's agent, an order for delivery of actual possession is unavailable while that arrangement stands.
